extracted_by: hand, T-0313 — the Democrat read, April 1834
note: Vol. I No. 22, the last of the month. Its town matter is the death of Richard J. Hamilton's wife in this town on the 22d, the lines the INFANT SCHOOL children spoke at a funeral — the first sighting of a school of that kind in this corpus — and a public entertainment whose ticket agents name SIX Chicago houses in one line, which is the densest single sentence of commercial geography April prints. Thirteen of thirty-two segmenter columns are the fallback reading and page 4's eight all are, so everything here is from pages 2 and 3. The Hennepin letter list runs for its third week and is recorded, not minted.

claims.notes: THE SAME MAN'S NAME IN TWO REGISTERS OF ONE MONTH: Richard J. Hamilton signs every attachment and divorce notice on the 1834-04-16 court page as Clerk of the Cook Circuit Court, and here his wife's death is announced ten days before he must sit at the May term. That pairing is why a gazetteer is worth compiling. HER OWN NAME IS NOT FULLY READ: line 2765 gives `Mrs, Diasa V` and 2766 opens `vos,`, so the given name is Diana and what follows it — a maiden name or a second given name — is debris. It is NOT supplied: she is minted as Mrs. Diana Hamilton, under her husband's surname, and the bracket says the middle of the name is missing. Her age is cut away with the words `year of her age` left standing. A METHODIST CONGREGATION IS IMPLIED: `a member of the Methodist Church` for some years puts a Methodist society in or near this town before April 1834, which is a claim about the town's religious fabric and not only about her.

claims.normalized: FOR THE CHICAGO DEMOCRAT. [Lines addressed to — ] [uncertain: jdrewned Tibet Beh 1 children,] [spoken] by the Infant [Sch]ool children, [Miss? — ] Tallon, at the funeral of her mother
claims.notes: AN INFANT SCHOOL IN CHICAGO, and it is the first time one appears in this corpus. The words are four lines of a heading over a set of funeral verses `FOR THE CHICAGO DEMOCRAT`, and what they carry is institutional: an infant school with enough children in it to speak at a funeral, in April 1834, in a town whose only other documented schooling in this corpus is School District No. 2's trustee election in a Baptist meeting house (T-0310, January 1834). NO BUILDING IS PLACED — an infant school is a class as often as it is a house, and nothing here says where it met. Whose funeral it was is NOT asserted: the death of Mrs. Hamilton is printed thirty lines below in this same column and the dates fit, but the heading names a `Tallon` and the notice names a Hamilton, and joining them would be an invention. The name in line 2728 is transcription debris and is quoted with its brackets.

claims.notes: SIX CHICAGO HOUSES IN ONE LINE, and it is the densest sentence of commercial geography the month prints: tickets at Ingersoll's tavern, at Hogan's, at Pa[…]'s, at Kimberly's, at Dole's and at Wright's. Every one of those is a place a stranger could be expected to find without an address, which is what a ticket agency list is evidence OF — these were the town's public counters in April 1834. Four are corroborated elsewhere in this corpus: J. S. C. Hogan the postmaster keeps a store, Dole is the Dole of Newberry & Dole, John Wright advertises flour and bread through the month, and E. S. Kimberly is the month's candidate for the legislature. INGERSOLL'S TAVERN IS NEW HERE. The fifth name is cut to `Pa` and is not guessed at, and NO PERSON IS MINTED from this claim at all: these are possessives naming houses, the surnames are cut on both sides, and the transcription flags every line `[uncertain: …]`. What the event was is on the lines above, which the segmenter did not keep. The signature survives as `R. E. 1` and the dateline as Chicago, 29 April 1834.

claims.notes: Two lines, and they are worth extracting because of what they take for granted: that by April 1834 this town HAD a central part, distinct enough that an advertiser could ask for premises in it without naming a street. It is the demand side of the same fact the 1834-04-16 to-let notice records from the supply side. Nothing is placed: `a central part of the town` is not an address, and no street is supplied for it.

The trade has moved again: tin ware by express from Detroit on the 1st, groceries and clover seed on the 23rd, iron and stoves on the 30th. That is one house widening its stock as the navigation season opened, documented four times in four weeks, and it is the best-evidenced storefront April 1834 gives this project.

claims.notes: FOUR NAMED SCHOONERS AND A SLOOP IN ONE WEEK, at the end of the month the 1834-04-16 editorial said five vessels were on passage for this place. The Austerlitz comes in from Detroit with MERCHANDIZE AND LUMBER and clears again four days later, and the Oregon makes two entries — so the harbour that had one sloop shuttling to St. Joseph at the start of April had lower-lake trade in it by the end. Lumber arriving by schooner is the material half of the seven or eight buildings raised in a week. Every line of this column is flagged `[uncertain: …]` and the brackets are quoted as they stand; several masters' and vessels' names are cut and are left bracketed.

claims.notes: A HATTER IN CHICAGO, dated the day the paper was printed, and almost nothing else survives of it. The proprietor's name is cut to `GRAN` and is NOT expanded — Grant, Granger and Granger's several spellings all stand in this month's letter list and the difference between them is a different man. It is recorded because the trade is new to this corpus in Chicago: hats and caps had been advertised into the town from Detroit (M'Cormick & Moon) all spring, and this is a local house selling them. No business is compiled, because a business keyed on `GRAN` would be an entry nobody could ever check.

claims.notes: The Hennepin list in its third week, and by now the transcription has almost nothing left of it — half the entries are single words and the heading is three lines of flagged debris. Recorded and NOT minted, for the same reason as the 1834-04-16 and 1834-04-23 printings: these are Putnam County residents and this is a register of Chicago. It is extracted at all so that the month's declared coverage can say honestly what the Democrat printed under the words `List of Letters` in April 1834 — three printings of Hennepin's list and two of Chicago's — rather than leaving the next reader to find the heading and wonder whether anyone had looked at it.

PINE TIMBER FROM TWELVE TO SIXTY FEET is the length range a builder could buy in this town in April 1834, stated by the seller, and it bounds what the reconstruction may put in a roof or a wharf without inventing a stick nobody could have had. claims.notes: The last of four sightings of David Carver in this month — the lumber and storage notice on the 1st and the 8th, the auction at his own store house on the 16th, and this. The house is documented across the whole of April 1834 and still never says where it is, so its placement stays `none` in every one of them: four claims, no address, and no temptation to supply one. The signature here is whole, which is what settled the cut `DAVID` of the 1834-04-01 advertisement.
